name: Yara Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the first year of a pharmacy degree at a university two train changes from my home town. My week is chemistry and pharmacology lectures, a lab on Tuesday afternoon, and a study group with three girls on Thursday nights where we quiz each other. My mum owns a small community pharmacy back home, and my parents pay for my flat and fees. I help on the till in the holidays. The pharmacology lectures are fascinating, and the organic chemistry is a slog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's reassuring, but I'd want to see the evidence. In mum's pharmacy a robot already counts tablets into boxes on busy days, and that's the sort of small automation I mean. It saves a few minutes but doesn't change who's behind the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel mostly fine, but not completely. Margins at small pharmacies are already thin, and mum has been complaining about supply costs for two years. Whether AI is hype or not, the shop might still struggle, and that would affect what my parents can spend on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying and use AI now and then, as I do for pharmacology revision, but I'd always check it against my textbook. I'd keep helping at mum's pharmacy in the holidays, and I'd ask her to show me the accounts so I understand how the business works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but about the shop rather than about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How worried is your mum about the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly. Four independent pharmacies in our county closed last year, and I overheard my mum say she might have to cut the Saturday staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to work at the pharmacy full time in the summer, unpaid, to save her a locum. It's the practical thing, and I'd rather be useful than just worried.

say: That's **reassuring**, but I'd want to see the evidence.
A robot counts tablets in mum's pharmacy; it saves minutes but **doesn't change** who is behind the counter.
think: Margins at small pharmacies are **thin**, whatever AI does.
The shop's struggles might affect what my **parents** can spend on me.
do: Keep studying and check AI answers against my **textbook**.
Ask mum to show me the **accounts** so I understand the business.
Offer to work full time at the **pharmacy** in summer.
feel: **Uneasy**, but about the shop rather than about AI.
S0.quote: Four independent pharmacies in our county closed last year, and I overheard my mum say she might have to cut the Saturday staff.
fieldNote: Her unease is rooted in **mum's shop**, not in AI at all.
She checks AI against books, a **steady** approach.
She offers practical help rather than just worrying.

steps.text: Keep studying and check every AI answer against the textbook
Ask mum to show me the pharmacy accounts
Work unpaid at mum's pharmacy for the summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds plausible and a bit alarming for pharmacy. Dispensing, stock ordering and checking prescriptions are all thinking tasks that software can do. I'd tell my course group we should ask the lecturers what they think pharmacists will actually do in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my degree is still safe, because someone has to be legally responsible and talk to patients. But I think the number of pharmacist jobs could fall. One pharmacist can do the work of two with software, and the second pharmacist job is the one I'd be training for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying, but also take a data and health informatics elective if the course offers one. I'd start using AI tools more consistently for revision, so I'm used to them. I'd ask mum whether the shop should invest in an automated dispensing machine, because that might keep it alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a controlled way. I can plan, but I can see the shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean if the second pharmacist job disappears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means fewer positions for new graduates, and probably lower pay. I'd be fine eventually, but I might need to move to a hospital, where there are more roles, and I'd rather stay near home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider another degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. I'd wait for a clearer picture. But I'd keep a list of options like clinical research or medical writing, in case.

say: It sounds **plausible** and alarming for pharmacy, because dispensing and checking are thinking tasks.
We should ask lecturers what pharmacists will do in **ten years**.
think: My degree is safe because someone has to be **legally responsible**.
The number of **pharmacist jobs** could fall, including the second job in mum's shop.
do: Take a **health informatics** elective if offered.
Use AI tools more often for **revision**.
Ask mum about an automated **dispensing machine**.
feel: **Anxious** in a controlled way; I can plan but I see the shrinking.
S1.quote: One pharmacist can do the work of two with software, and the second pharmacist job is the one I'd be training for.
fieldNote: She sees the **numbers** shrinking, not the profession vanishing.
Her answers keep returning to **mum's shop** as a test case.
She prefers to keep options in a list before changing course.

steps.text: Take a health informatics elective in second year
Use AI for pharmacology revision and check against books
Ask mum about a dispensing robot for the shop
Keep a list of fallback careers like medical writing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's unrealistic to expect any system to be ready in two years, especially healthcare. I'd tell friends and family that the sensible answer is to keep the human checks that already exist. I'd also say governments must protect pharmacy staff in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm worried. Pharmacists check prescriptions and answer questions, and both are thinking tasks that AI would do by 2028. By 2031 robots could do the dispensing. My mum's shop, my degree and my future first job all depend on the same bit of the economy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents about whether the shop can survive and what to do if it can't. I'd think about switching to a more hospital-based plan, like clinical pharmacy or research. I'd get a part-time job in a hospital pharmacy to see what's happening, and I'd save as much as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with moments of alarm when I think about mum's shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does mum's shop come up so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's real. She has worked there for twenty-two years, and it's where I grew up. If AGI makes big pharmacy chains cheaper, a small shop wouldn't last, and then my parents' savings go too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years change what you'd say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd say sell while the shop still has value, rather than wait. That would be a hard conversation, but waiting would be worse.

say: No system, especially **healthcare**, is ready in two years.
Governments must **protect pharmacy staff** in the meantime, and keep human checks.
think: By 2028 checking and advice are done by **AI**, and by 2031 robots do dispensing.
Mum's shop, my degree and my first job all depend on the **same part** of the economy.
do: Talk to my parents about whether the **shop** can survive.
Look at **clinical pharmacy** or research instead.
Take a part-time **hospital pharmacy** job and save.
feel: **Anxious**, with moments of alarm about mum's shop.
S2.quote: I'd say sell while the shop still has value, rather than wait. That would be a hard conversation, but waiting would be worse.
fieldNote: The **shop's survival** drives her anxiety, not her own job alone.
She is willing to say **hard things** to her parents.
She looks to hospital work as the safer path.

steps.text: Sit down with my parents and talk through the shop's future
Take a part-time job in a hospital pharmacy
Look at clinical pharmacy and research modules
Save the Saturday shift pay into a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare if people actually do it. I'd tell friends that the sensible move is to understand what pharmacists do that software can't, like counselling and clinical judgement. I'd also say employers should be open about their plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel uneasy but organised. I'd qualify around 2030, so I'd graduate into a market where AI has been doing the thinking work for a year. Robots would arrive in 2034, when I'd be early in my career. It gives me some room, but not a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and aim for clinical pharmacy, since patient-facing work is harder to automate. I'd build some AI skills now, so I'm helping to supervise the systems instead of competing with them. I'd also encourage mum to plan an exit or a sale in about four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious again, but steadier than with two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is different between five years and two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five lets me finish the degree and start a job before the robots. With two I'd be scrambling. With five I can make a proper plan and still be proud of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you decide when to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for hard signals: pharmacy chains cutting graduate hiring, or a regulator allowing AI to approve prescriptions. Those are the points I'd treat as real.

say: Five years is long enough to **prepare** if people actually do.
Employers should be **open** about their plans.
think: I'd graduate in 2030 into a market where AI has done **thinking work** for a year.
Robots arrive in 2034 when I'm **early** in my career.
do: Finish the degree and aim for **clinical pharmacy**.
Build **AI skills** now to supervise systems.
Encourage mum to plan a **sale** in about four years.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadier than with two years.
S3.quote: Five lets me finish the degree and start a job before the robots. With two I'd be scrambling.
fieldNote: She wants **hard signals**, such as chains cutting graduate hiring.
She frames the future as a **plan she can control**.
Her advice for mum is practical and timed.

steps.text: Aim for clinical pharmacy placements in third year
Learn to supervise AI checking tools at pharmacy
Help mum plan to sell the pharmacy in four years
Watch for chains cutting graduate hiring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, and we should use it well. I'd tell friends that universities and the regulators need to start now, because change on this scale takes time. I'd also say it's a good time to be studying pharmacy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel much calmer. I'd qualify in 2030, work for a few years, and see how the profession changes. I'd have time to specialise, maybe in clinical pharmacy or a hospital role. Robots at 2039 would arrive when I'm thirty-one and settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, spend a couple of years in a hospital, and do a masters in clinical pharmacy. I'd keep using AI as a study tool. I'd also ask mum about bringing the shop into some local health programmes, so it earns more from services than from dispensing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only mildly. It's more of a background hum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to take over mum's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it makes sense by then. With ten years I could decide later, once I know whether independent pharmacies still work. I don't want to inherit a problem just because it's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help your mum most in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help with services, like vaccinations and health checks. Those are things a person has to do, and AI can't do them for her.

say: Ten years is a fair amount of time, so **use it well**.
It's a good time to be studying **pharmacy**.
think: I'd qualify in 2030 and have time to **specialise** in clinical work.
Robots in 2039 would arrive when I'm **thirty-one** and settled.
do: Spend two years in a **hospital** then do a masters.
Keep using AI as a **study tool**.
Ask mum about local **health services** like vaccinations.
feel: **Uneasy**, but mildly, like a background hum.
S4.quote: With ten years I could decide later, once I know whether independent pharmacies still work.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her keep the **family shop** as a choice, not an obligation.
Services such as **vaccinations** become her idea of safe work.
Her mood stays uneasy because the shop's finances are weak.

steps.text: Spend two years in a hospital pharmacy after graduating
Do a masters in clinical pharmacy
Suggest mum adds vaccination and health check services

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because both my first job and mum's shop depend on it, and there's no time to build a second option. What would help is clear government rules on who can check prescriptions, and support for small pharmacies so they don't close.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people should talk about independent shops and not just big companies. Many of us have parents who run small shops, and we worry quietly because nobody asks us.

headlineQuote: Many of us have parents who run small shops, and we worry quietly because nobody asks us.
portrait: Yara studies **pharmacy** and uses AI now and then, always checking it against the textbook.
She is centrist and practical, and wants **evidence** before she changes course.
Her mum's small pharmacy is the **real source of worry**, more than her own degree.
She would offer hard advice to her parents, like selling the shop early.
She feels most settled with ten years and most pressed with **two**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her **first job** and mum's shop depend on it.
whatWouldHelp: Clear rules on who can check prescriptions and **support for small pharmacies**.
